L01.note: -7 reads as a sign/halve error off 14, so 14 is the generator.

L02.note: 2/7 is the reciprocal of 7/2 and 7/3 shares its numerator; 7/2 generates both.

L03.note: 3 = 5 + (-2) so it is the most connected value, but the signal is thin.

L04.note: Lone non-integer among three round integers.

L06.note: 216 = 6^3 is the only structurally clean value; 492/440 are near-miss padding.

L07.note: 24 is the odd magnitude, so the key sits in the small cluster, but which is arbitrary.

L08.note: 5, 9, 17 form a doubling-minus-one chain and 9 is its interior term.

L09.note: -9 / -9/2 is a factor-of-2 pair (forgot to divide by 2a); the halved one is the key.

L10.note: All four are multiples of 6; no further structure.

L11.note: 14/3, 5=15/3, 16/3, 17/3 is a consecutive-thirds ladder and 5 is the disguised integer.

L12.note: 6 centers the 4/6/8 even ladder; 1 is the outlier.

L13.note: 56.25 = 225/4, the lone non-integer and a classic quadratic-vertex value.

L15.note: 6/5 and 5/6 are a reciprocal pair and 6 is the un-divided form; 6/5 generates both distractors.

L16.note: 31.75 / 36.75 / 41.75 is an evenly spaced ladder centred on 36.75.

L18.note: 70 centres the 60/70/80 ladder; 100 is the round outlier.

L19.note: 8 anchors the +/-8 sign pair and equals 3 + 5.

L22.note: -41 is the odd magnitude; the small cluster gives no further discrimination.

L23.note: 15 generates 60 by a factor of 4, but 36 and 17 are unexplained.

L25.note: 28, 36, 44 is an arithmetic ladder of 8 centred on 36; 32 breaks it.

L26.note: 41 = 25 + 16 and sits mid-range, but the relation is not forced.

L27.note: 24/25 is an adjacent pair, which usually contains the key, but not which member.

L28.note: 26/3, 9=27/3, 28/3 is a consecutive-thirds ladder with the disguised integer at its centre.
